doc.title: Jackie McLean — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The record shop, trading the soprano for an alto, and first hearing Bird
summary: McLean disliked the straight soprano, got an alto at 15, was steered to Hodges and Tab Smith but was drawn to tenors, until he heard Charlie Parker on a Trummy Young record in the shop.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: What was the name of this shop?
It was just a record shop. I can’t remember. Briggs, or something like that. We didn’t even have a name. It was just a record shop.
It was bigger than this. It was huge, about four of these rooms. So he – I would be in there, opening up records. He would – finally I got an alto, when I was 15.
This came to you through your mother?
Yeah, and him. They bought me an alto.
Tell us – how did that – what was the thing? You just didn’t like the soprano?

No, I didn’t want the soprano, because after I went and looked, saw all these guys playing these big, beautiful, curved saxophones, man, I’d look at this thing. And then there were some guys in my neighborhood who played music, and they all had horns. I had this . . .
Yeah, that wasn’t a horn, because it didn’t have a curve in it.
No, man. It wasn’t – it didn’t count to me. Every time I even took it out, I was like, looking around. I didn’t want anybody to see.
Yeah, right. So they bought me a saxophone, an alto, when I was 15. Then . . .
Did you want an alto or tenor?

I didn’t know the difference at that point. I really wasn’t familiar. I just wanted a curved one, a gold one. So they bought me an alto, which was the most inexpensive one. Then I was in the back room, trying to play this record now of Lester Young and copy what he’s playing. My dad came in – my stepfather came in and said, “Hey, you can’t play that on that, man.” He says, “Here’s how you got to sound.” He took me out

and let me hear Johnny Hodges. I listened to Johnny Hodges. I was like, yeah. Then he played Tab Smith, another alto player with a big, sweet, syrupy sound. Then he played Willie Smith for me. All of these people, I really – I wasn’t drawn to. I was drawn to the tenor players. So then one day we were down in the record shop. We opened up some records, and I pulled out a record and put it on, by Trummy Young, and that’s when I first heard Bird. When I heard that, I told him – I said, “That’s an alto.” So he said, “That ain’t no alto.” He said, “No, that ain’t no alto.” So I said, “Yeah, that is an alto.” Then when the record was over, he looked on there, and it’s Charlie Parker. Then we opened up another box of records, and there was the Savoy recordings of Now’s the Time and Billie’s Bounce. So that’s how I – through the record shop, I got introduced to a lot.
